summary: Explaining industrialisation and the Great Divergence: Joel Mokyr, E. A. Wrigley, Jan de Vries and R. Bin Wong become person entries, promoted from existing people records. Mokyr: useful knowledge (to technology), the Industrial Enlightenment and, with Kelly and Ó Gráda, skills against high wages (to the debate), and his 2002 critique of Pomeranz. Wrigley: the population reconstruction with Schofield (to demography), the organic economy (to the debate), his influence on Wong, and readers’ comparison of his coal with Pomeranz’s. De Vries: the industrious revolution (to the debate), its use by Pomeranz, the Dutch Republic as the first modern economy (to economic), the Cambridge Group’s influence on him, and his case for demand against Mokyr’s supply-side view. Wong: reciprocal comparison taken up by Pomeranz, political fragmentation and war with Rosenthal (to the debate), and his 2016 critique of Brenner. The 1.145 arrows drawn for them from demography, consumption and technology (edges 1084–1086) are re-sourced to the new entries, keeping their ids, and Mokyr leaves edge_1050 for his own arrow. Two source links are corrected, to an author-posted copy and a DOI.

rationale: The 1.145 debate entry left Mokyr, Wrigley, de Vries and Wong as roster rows and drew their component contributions from fields “for now”. Each now has at least three edges and at least eight dated points. Mokyr, Wrigley and de Vries each have at least three points read in their own words. Wong has two independently read texts in his own words (the chapter openings of China Transformed and “Divergence Displaced”, 2016); his 2011 point rests on his own 2016 summary and Ma’s review. Every person therefore meets the rule of at least two edges and three timeline points backed by read evidence. Every edge rests on a text read in the person’s own words (author-posted papers, publisher excerpts, Cambridge Core openings and abstracts, an open-access article) or on a named reader’s explicit statement; unread books (The Gifts of Athena, The Enlightened Economy, A Culture of Growth, Before and Beyond Divergence) are given only through named reviewers or their authors’ later summaries. Source links are official: DOIs, publisher pages and excerpts, the authors’ own postings and open-access journal or repository copies. The new jan_de_vries entry and the revised edge_1085 quote de Vries (1994) only from its publisher abstract; previously accepted page-based claims from that article remain. The Mokyr 1999 essay was re-read in his own posted copy. Nothing is drawn twice: edges 1084–1086 change source rather than gaining twins, and Mokyr’s critique of Pomeranz leaves edge_1050. Weak or thin links are left out (see each draft’s edges_considered_not_proposed).

edge_1050.relationship: Broadberry and Gupta place the advanced parts of Asia with Europe's stagnating periphery on wages and prices (2006); Vries finds differences, not 'surprising resemblances' (2009); Allen and colleagues dispute Chinese–English urban real-wage parity (2011); Broadberry, Guan and Li place divergence between leading regions around 1700 (2021)
edge_1050.map_label: Wages, the state and regional GDP, 2006–2021
edge_1050.evidence_note: This arrow represents named interventions within the debate entry, not a verdict of it; the entry includes Pomeranz and his allies, and each intervention establishes something different. Broadberry and Gupta (EHR 59:1, 2006; summary and pp. 2–3 read), on wages and prices: "Contrary to the claims of Pomeranz, Parthasarathi, and other 'world historians', the prosperous parts of Asia between 1500 and 1800 look similar to the stagnating southern, central, and eastern parts of Europe … The 'great divergence' … was already well underway before 1800" (p. 2). Vries ('A World of Surprising Resemblances?', 2009, pp. 35–38, 47–48 read), on agriculture and the state: 'I would not call that a "surprising resemblance"' (p. 38); 'Coal and colonies definitely were fundamental in the Rise of the West. But reference to them cannot suffice to explain it' (p. 48). Allen, Bassino, Ma, Moll-Murata and van Zanden (EHR 2011, read pp. 8–9, 29–31), on urban real wages: 'our findings also dispute the revisionists’ claim that the advanced parts of China, such as the Yangzi Delta, were on a par with England'; 'Adam Smith’s pessimism looks closer to the truth than the revisionists’ optimism' (p. 31); they also find Chinese urban wages on a par with central and southern Europe, against the 'rise of the west' literature (pp. 30–31). Broadberry, Guan and Li (JEH 2021, read pp. 958–959), on regional GDP per capita: 'The Great Divergence thus began around 1700, earlier than originally suggested by the California School, but later than implied by earlier writers' (p. 958); the qualified chronology is theirs alone. None endorses Huang's involution, whose dispute with Pomeranz is drawn on its own arrows. Revision 1.145 moved this arrow from economic to the debate entry capitalismdebates, and moved Brenner and Isett's 2002 critique to its own arrow (robert_brenner → kenneth_pomeranz), as this note had foreseen. Revision 1.146 likewise moved Mokyr's 2002 critique to its own arrow (joel_mokyr → kenneth_pomeranz), since Mokyr became a person entry; the four interventions above remain.

edge_1086.relationship: Useful knowledge as the cause of sustained growth: the “Industrial Enlightenment”, “the key to sustained and accelerating invention” (2002 draft), which kept the early Industrial Revolution from “fizzling out” (2007 lecture); with Kelly and Ó Gráda, British workers’ human capital against Allen’s high-wage explanation (2014), and low initial wages and mechanical skills across England’s 41 counties (2023)
edge_1086.evidence_note: His own words, read. October 2002 draft (“The Enduring Riddle of the European Miracle”, p. 10): Enlightenment thinkers “created the attitudes, the institutions, and the mechanisms by which new knowledge was created, spread and put to good use. It is this specific aspect of the period that I have called the Industrial Enlightenment … the movement was not the key to invention; it was the key to sustained and accelerating invention.” Max Weber Lecture (EUI, 2007, pp. 2–5): countries of the 1914 “convergence club” “were countries that in the eighteenth century were subject to the European Enlightenment. This strong correlation is not in and of itself proof of causality” (p. 2); the tightening of propositional and prescriptive knowledge “prevented the early Industrial Revolution from fizzling out and enabled it to become the taproot of modern growth” (p. 5). With Morgan Kelly and Cormac Ó Gráda, “Precocious Albion” (2014, author-posted proof, pp. 16.2–16.4): “the main reason for its precocity was its higher level of human capital”; against Allen’s induced innovation, “the driver of technological progress was something deeper and stronger than cheap coal and high wages”. “The Mechanics of the Industrial Revolution” (JPE 2023, pp. 60–61): their prediction “runs directly counter to the influential argument of Allen (2009a)”; the finding concerns the 41 counties of England, not Britain’s international position. The Enlightened Economy (2009) is unread; reviewing it, Harley (EH.Net, 2010, read) wondered “if causation from Enlightenment, as an intellectual stance, to economic change actually existed” and found that it “seems almost to describe the nature of successful change at least as much as its cause.” Each quotation is tied to the text it comes from; the 2002 wording is not claimed for the 2009 book. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from technology because Mokyr had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to joel_mokyr and keeps its id. His theory of useful knowledge as such is drawn on joel_mokyr → technology.

edge_1084.relationship: The Industrial Revolution as escape from an “organic economy” bounded by land: growth from two sets of forces with “only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time” (1988), the question “why it did not come to an end”, without dismissing institutional or scientific explanations (2010), and coal as “the solution” (2016); Berg and Hudson questioned causal inference from Wrigley and Schofield’s aggregate studies (1990)
edge_1084.evidence_note: His own words, in Cambridge University Press excerpts. Continuity, Chance and Change (1988, pp. 1–8 read in revision 1.145): “After many years spent in work principally concerned with the population history of England, I had returned increasingly to my first main research interest, the better understanding of the industrial revolution” (p. 1); “My main aim in the lectures was to question the appropriateness of the view that the industrial revolution was a cumulative, progressive, unitary phenomenon” (p. 3); growth was “the product of two different sets of forces having only an accidental relationship to one another in the early stages of their overlap in time” (p. 4); the classical economists remain authoritative for “an economy bounded by the productivity of the land, what I shall term an organic economy” (p. 5). Energy and the English Industrial Revolution (2010, pp. 1–6, 9–11 read): “the most important single issue on which to focus in trying to gain a clearer understanding of the industrial revolution is not how the period of more rapid growth began, but why it did not come to an end” (p. 4); “the production horizon for all organic economies was set by the annual cycle of plant growth” (p. 9); “There can be no single, ‘true’ account of the industrial revolution” (p. 4); institutional and scientific explanations get “only glancing references”, but “it would be both presumptuous and mildly ridiculous to downplay their importance”, and the explanations are “essentially incommensurable” (pp. 4–5). The Path to Sustained Growth (2016, p. 3): “Mining coal provided the solution to this problem.” Poverty, Progress, and Population (2004, pp. 1–3): Rostow’s “take-off” is “now almost impossible to maintain” (p. 2), and Berg and Hudson put the counter-view “vigorously and effectively” (p. 3 n. 6). The 2013 article is read in abstract only. Critique: Berg and Hudson (1990 working paper, read): “The work of Wrigley and Schofield dominates the population history of this period and illustrates some of the more general problems of causal analysis based on aggregative studies.” Their objection concerns causal inference from the aggregate series, not the reconstruction as such. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from demography because Wrigley had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to e_a_wrigley and keeps its id. His population reconstruction is drawn on e_a_wrigley → demography.

edge_1085.relationship: The “industrious revolution”: a household-level, demand-side change that preceded the supply-side Industrial Revolution (1994), built on the revision that cut British growth estimates “by more than half” and dated to roughly 1650–1850 (2008); reviewers asked whether consumption had become a new “deus ex machina” (2009), and papermaking evidence challenged its chronology and mechanism (2016)
edge_1085.evidence_note: His own words, read. JEH 1994, abstract (Cambridge Core): “The Industrial Revolution as a historical concept has many shortcomings. A new concept—the ‘industrious revolution’—is proposed to place the Industrial Revolution in a broader historical setting … The industrious revolution was a household-level change with important demand-side features that preceded the Industrial Revolution, a supply-side phenomenon.” The Industrious Revolution (2008, publisher excerpt, pp. 6–10): “the accumulating evidence for an earlier increase of per capita income in northwestern Europe paired with a major refinement of material life casts serious doubt on the orthodoxy that the Industrial Revolution was the actual starting point for long-term economic growth” (pp. 6–7); among the literatures that “guided my thinking” is “The Revisionist Macroeconomics of the British Industrial Revolution”, which “reduces the earlier growth estimates by more than half” (pp. 7–8, citing Crafts and Harley 1992); the approach would “question the claims of the twin revolutions – the British Industrial and the French political – to function as gatekeepers to modern history” (p. 9); households “acted to reallocate their productive resources (which are chiefly the time of their members)” during “a long eighteenth century, roughly 1650–1850” (p. 10). Reviewers, read: Voth (EH.Net, 2009) finds the book “on all the main points, convincing”, with “the almost complete disconnect with behavioral economics” as its weakness; van Nederveen Meerkerk (TSEG, 2009) finds that consumption becomes “een nieuwe ‘deus ex machina’” (p. 176). Rosenband (2016, abstract): papermaking raises “fundamental challenges to this model”; “paperworkers already labored exhausting hours at the outset of de Vries's period of newfound industriousness”, and “women and adolescent workers toiled for wages in paper mills long before the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries”. The 1994 article’s pages read in earlier revisions are not quoted here. Revision 1.145 drew this arrow from consumption because de Vries had no entry; revision 1.146 re-sources it to jan_de_vries and keeps its id. Pomeranz’s use of the concept is now on jan_de_vries → kenneth_pomeranz; the household mechanism stays on consumption/household_labor.
